lesson.title: One Party, Uneasy Peace: America's Brief Era of Good Feelings
lesson.summary: With the Federalist Party dead after the War of 1812, James Monroe presided over a period of surface political unity that masked growing arguments over the economy and slavery.
lesson.body:
The Era of Good Feelings describes the period of American politics roughly from 1817 to the mid-1820s, when the collapse of the Federalist Party after the War of 1812 left the Democratic-Republicans as the only serious national party. A Boston newspaper, the Columbian Centinel, coined the phrase during President James Monroe's goodwill tour of New England in 1817, a region that had been a Federalist stronghold and a center of resistance to the recent war.

Monroe, a Virginian who had served as a diplomat, senator, and secretary of state and war under Madison, won the presidency in 1816 over a badly weakened Federalist opponent. He was reelected in 1820 by an overwhelming electoral margin, and according to a popular story, one New Hampshire elector, William Plumer, cast the only dissenting vote so that George Washington would remain the only president ever elected unanimously, though some historians argue Plumer simply preferred another candidate. Either way, the near unanimous result reflected how thoroughly one party politics had taken hold.

Beneath the label of good feelings, though, real arguments continued over how the growing nation should develop. Henry Clay promoted a set of policies he called the American System: a protective tariff to shield young American manufacturers from British competition, a national bank to stabilize currency and credit, and federally funded roads and canals to tie the country's regions together economically. Congress chartered the Second Bank of the United States in 1816 and passed a protective tariff that same year, both building on the war's lesson that the country needed a stronger, more self sufficient economy.

That economic confidence cracked in 1819. Loose lending and speculative land purchases in the West, encouraged in part by the Second Bank's own branches, fed a bubble that burst when the bank tightened credit to protect its reserves. The Panic of 1819 brought bank failures, farm foreclosures, and unemployment, and it was the first major financial crisis in the young republic's history. It also sharpened resentment of the national bank in the newer western states, a resentment that would resurface loudly a decade later under Andrew Jackson.

The deeper crack in the era's surface calm was slavery. As Missouri Territory applied for statehood in 1819, Congress found itself sharply divided over whether to allow slavery to expand into new western territories, a fight that produced the Missouri Compromise of 1820. The very name Era of Good Feelings, then, describes a political style built around a single dominant party more than it describes genuine national unity, and the sectional and economic tensions simmering underneath would shape the next several decades of American politics, including the foreign policy statement Monroe issued in 1823 that came to be called the Monroe Doctrine.
